John Janusas’s first Saugus team finished 7–3 and No. 5 in the final Class B standings with 54 rating points and a 5.40 average. After falling one foot short of the goal line in a 12–6 opening loss to Brookline, the Sachems won five straight. Earl Dudman’s 86-yard punt return set up his sneak in the 20–0 Swampscott win, and Fred Quinlan ran 66 yards for a touchdown against Marblehead. Dudman played in the Massachusetts All-Star game. Laskey was selected for that game, did not play, and made the Class B team with tackle Eugene Decereau.

Mike Ginolfi’s Sachems went 9–1 and shared the Northeastern Conference title. They posted six shutouts and won their last six games after losing to Swampscott. Against Salem, Saugus trailed 14–0 at halftime. An 80-yard, 18-play drive ended with Jay LeBranti’s 25-yard touchdown pass to Frank Scuzzarella on third-and-19 with 47 seconds left. John Nicolo ran for 134 yards on 29 carries and kicked the extra point for the 15–14 win.

In the Thanksgiving Mud Bowl, Steve Gannon blocked a Peabody field goal and Nicolo returned it for the only touchdown in a 6–0 win. The Item named Nicolo its football Player of the Year. Doug Mackie earned Parade All-American honors and All-Scholastic recognition from the Boston Globe and the Herald American/Herald Advertiser.

Steve Peach completed 14 of 27 passes for 245 yards and two touchdowns, ran for two more and kicked the extra point that made the difference. After Classical pulled within a point with 11 seconds left, Peach knocked down Tony Thurman’s two-point pass.

history: A Brief History of Saugus High Football
Introduction

Saugus High School’s football program boasts over a century of tradition marked by unforgettable triumphs, legendary players, and the unyielding spirit of a small-town community in Massachusetts. From its humble beginnings in the early 1900s to its golden era of state championships, the Sachems have woven a rich tapestry of history that continues to inspire “Sachem Pride” to this day. This overview traces the program’s key eras, coaches, stars, and milestones, celebrating its enduring legacy despite recent challenges.
1900–1919 (The Early Years):
J.W. Stanley (1901)

The season archive’s earliest listed Saugus High team is the 1901 squad, coached by J. W. Stanley and featuring Chas Bennett. A separate 1896 gallery clipping reports a Saugus football team without explicitly identifying it as Saugus High School. The archive resumes its regular season chronology in 1914; gaps in the surviving material should not be treated as proof that no football was played.
Arthur L. William (1914)

Saugus High has fielded a football team in most seasons since 1914. The 1914 team was coached by Arthur L. William. Saugus went 2-7 during Coach Williams’ lone season as Head Coach. The team was led by players John Fox and George Sprague.
Charles T. Senay (1915-1916)

Charles T. Senay guided Saugus High through two of the strongest early seasons preserved in the football archive. His 1915 team finished undefeated at 6–0, and the 1916 squad followed with a 7–1 record. Together, the two teams went 13–1, establishing an impressive standard for the young program. George Sprague, John Flynn, and Mike Garofano are among the players named in the surviving season records. Both teams competed in the Greater Lynn League, although no championship has yet been verified for either year. Contemporary Saugus town reports also illustrate the school's growing commitment to athletics: the 1915 report praised the football program's progress during the preceding fall, while the 1916 report described improved school spirit and the creation of an Athletic Council. These reports provide historical context rather than independent confirmation of the 1915–1916 scores or a title.
Edward Collier (1917)

The season records list Edward Collier’s 1917 team at 0–5. No coach or season record is established for 1918 in this collection. The interruption’s cause has not been verified; the wartime and influenza context alone does not establish an explanation.
1920–1950: (The Golden Years):

The period from 1920 through 1950 is widely regarded as the “Golden Era” of Saugus football. During that stretch, Saugus won state championships in 1941 and 1944 and Exchange Bowl championships in 1949 and 1950, and produced several other teams that were strong enough to be considered among the best in program history.
Fred Beresford (1920–1922, 1928)

Fred Beresford’s 1922 Sachems finished unbeaten at 9–0–2, led by Franklin “Ooze” Pike, John Pike, Forrest Kenerson, Podge Herold, Lester Pool and Googie Emery. The season is listed as Greater Lynn League Champions. The historical title requires qualification: the 1942 yearbook retrospectively refers to a 1922 Class C championship, while an in-season newspaper clipping says Beresford was claiming no title at that point. Final contemporary championship documentation remains unresolved.

Championship spotlight — 1922: Fred Beresford's unbeaten 1922 team completed a remarkable 9–0–2 campaign. Franklin “Ooze” Pike, John Pike, Googie Emery, Forrest Kenerson, Podge Herold and Lester Pool helped establish an early winning tradition. The archive identifies the team as Greater Lynn League champions, while a 1942 yearbook retrospectively calls it a Class C championship team. Because a surviving in-season report said no title was being claimed at that point, the precise championship designation is presented with that historical qualification.
William Bangs (1923–1925)

William Bangs took over in 1923 and coached through 1925. Bangs maintained competitiveness but did not produce a winning season, finishing 6–6 in his final year. Some notable players on those Bangs teams were Pool and Emery, as well as Ernest Belliveau, Homer McNutt, Wally Guatreau, and Danton Sawyer.

Albion Rice coached in 1926–1927 and returned for 1929–1934 after Fred Beresford’s 1928 season. The archive lists a 7–4 finish in 1927, a 0–9 record in 1928 and a 7–2 season in 1931. The gallery’s 1928 review highlights captain Reggie Goss, Gilman Cann, Carroll Freeman, Red Hunnewell, Stuart Kidder and Jim Foley, including a long Kidder-to-Goss pass in the Thanksgiving loss to Mission High. Its 1929 account records victories over Manchester and Swampscott, while the 1930 pages celebrate captain Jim Muzzy, also spelled Muzzey, and Laurie Templeman. The 1931 season entry names George Riley, Joe Nelson, Malcolm Bisbee, Harry Gates, Red Doherty and Joe Scarozza.
John “Jack” Leahy (1935–1936)

John “Jack” Leahy took over the Sachems for the 1935 and 1936 seasons. Saugus had a very good 1935 season going 6-3. Some notable players from that 1935 team were Gerard Brazis, Phillip Hallam, Warren Vatcher, and Burton Norton. The 1936 Saugus team however dropped to 2-7-1.

Throughout its history, Saugus has primarily been known as the Sachems, a nickname that began during the Leahy era. Prior to the Sachems nickname and mascot, Saugus used other nicknames including Warriors (1914–1929) and Eagles (1930–1934).
Charles “Buzz” Harvey (1937–1940)

Charles “Buzz” Harvey coached Saugus from 1937 through 1940. His 1939 team finished 9–1–1 and won the North Shore championship, as recalled in the 1942 yearbook and corroborated by the contemporary town report. Co-captains Jimmy Duffy and Stan Green led a team featuring Mike Harrington, Art Statuto, Eddie Shipulski and their teammates. The gallery recounts the 3–0 victory over Salem and the 38–6 Thanksgiving win over Danvers, followed by a celebratory trip to New York and West Point. The town report places Saugus second in Class C; this regional championship should not be described as a verified 1939 state title.

Championship spotlight — 1939: Charles “Buzz” Harvey and assistant Nicholas Morris built a North Shore championship team whose success attracted statewide attention. After an opening loss to Medford, Saugus went unbeaten the rest of the season, including a tie with powerful Melrose and a memorable 3–0 victory over Salem. The 1939 school report credited Saugus as the second-highest-scoring team in Massachusetts and second in the Class C standings among 51 teams. The School Committee celebrated the achievement with a five-day educational trip to New York City. The North Shore title is documented; the town report does not award Saugus the Class C state championship.
Henry “Hammering Hank” Toczylowski (1941–1942)

Coach Harvey was succeeded by Henry “Hammering Hank” Toczylowski, a rising football star who had been drafted by the NFL’s Brooklyn Dodgers in 1941. Despite the opportunity to pursue a professional career, Toczylowski chose instead to coach and teach at Saugus High School. At the time of his hiring, he was a recent graduate of Boston College. In his senior season at Boston College in 1940, Toczylowski served as starting quarterback and team captain of the undefeated “Team of Destiny,” which finished 11–0. The Eagles recorded six shutouts and capped their season with a victory in the Sugar Bowl. He played under legendary coach Frank Leahy, who later won multiple national championships at Notre Dame (1943, 1946–47, 1949). Toczylowski was also named a First-Team All-American that season.

In his first year as head coach at Saugus in 1941, Toczylowski led the Sachems to a 10–0–1 record and the Class C state championship. The team featured several standout players previously coached by Harvey, including Statuto and Harrington, as well as Dick Macdonald, Eddie “Shipper” Shipulski, and Eddie Koschei. Harrington was a 2-time Football Captain for the Sachems. He was named to the Boston Herald, Boston Globe, WESX, and North Shore All Scholastic team his senior season. He also excelled as a baseball player. Unfortunately, his athletic career was cut short after his senior year due to an accident. Statuto went on to become a member of Notre Dame’s 1946 and 1947 national championship teams and played professionally for the Buffalo Bills in All American Football Conference and the Los Angeles Rams of the NFL. Toczylowski followed up with a 7–3–1 season in 1942 before stepping down to serve in World War II. He is a member of the Massachusetts High School Football Coaches Association Hall of Fame.

Championship spotlight — 1941: Henry “Hammering Hank” Toczylowski's 1941 Sachems finished 10–0–1 and captured the Massachusetts Class C state championship. Mike “Iron Mike” Harrington, Art Statuto, Eddie Shipulski and their teammates carried forward the program's emerging tradition of exceptional football. The superintendent's contemporary report celebrated the entire squad and specifically praised Toczylowski and fellow coach Edward Galligan, underscoring how much the championship meant to the school and community.
Dave Lucey (1943–1946)

Dave Lucey, another former member of the undefeated 1940 Boston College Eagles Football team and was a back up to Coach Toczylowski on that team, was hired to replace Coach Toczylowski in 1943 and would coach the Sachems through 1946. Coach Lucey guided Saugus to its greatest season, a 10–0 regular-season Class B championship run in 1944. The yearbook separately records a 19–7 postseason loss to Class A champion Peabody. During the 1944 Championship season, Saugus scored 207 points while only allowing 19. The 1944 team had many great players such as Art Spinney, Dick Allen, Bob Kane, Don Reiniger, Bruce Waybright, and Frank Pyzsko. Pyzsko was named Boston Globe and Post All Scholastic. Art Spinney, one of the greatest football players to ever come of Massachusetts, was named to several All-State teams; In 2024 he would be named to the Boston Globes All-Time All-Scholastic Football Team. Spinney would go on to play collegiately at Boston College where he was a four-year starter and named captain during his senior season. Spinney would be inducted into the Boston College Athletic Hall of Fame in 1972. After college, Spinney was drafted by Baltimore Colts of the NFL in 1950, however he only played in two games during his rookie season before he would be drafted into Army to fight in the Korean War. Spinney would miss the rest of the 1950 season and all of the 1951 and 1952 season due to his military service. In 1953 Spinney signed with the Cleveland Browns as a free agent, however he would be traded to the Baltimore Colts before the season. The Colts were an expansion team in 1953 as the 1950 Baltimore Colts Franchise had folded after the 1950 season. Spinney would play for the Colts from 1953 through 1960. Spinney was a 3-time All Pro (1958-1960), 2-time Pro Bowler (1959-1960) and 2-time NFL Champion (1958-1959). Some of Spinney’s teammates during his seasons with the Colts were Pro Football Hall of Famers Raymond Berry, Art Donovan, Gino Marchetti, Lenny Moore, Jim Parker, Johnn Unitas, and Don Shula. Spinney would retire from the NFL in 1960. Doug Waybright was another legend from the Lucey era. Waybright went on to play College Football at Notre Dame (1945, 1947–1949), as listed in his alumni profile. He was a member of the 1947 and 1949 National Championship teams (along with former Sachem teammate Art Statuto) while playing for Notre Dame. After college he served in the military before he returned to Saugus, where he was very active in youth sports. He was so beloved by the town that when he passed away at the young age of 38, officials named an elementary school in his honor.

Championship spotlight — 1944: Under Dave Lucey, the 1944 Sachems ran through ten regular-season games without a loss to earn the Massachusetts Class B championship. The archive records a dominant 207 points scored and only 19 allowed during that championship run. Art Spinney, Dick Allen, Bob Kane, Don Reiniger, Doug Waybright and Frank Pyszko were among its standouts. The yearbook also documents a separate 19–7 postseason loss to Class A champion Peabody, which does not erase the team's Class B title. The 1944 town report remembered 1939, 1941 and 1944 as three defining championship seasons.
1947–1960: (The Janusas Era):
John Janusas (1947–1960)

John Janusas coached Saugus from 1947 through 1960. His teams won consecutive Exchange Bowls in 1949 and 1950, followed by the North Shore League championship in 1953 and the North Shore League Champions designation for 1959. The 1953 title is explicit in the yearbook. The school district’s championship-banner announcement recognizes the 1959 team, although a contemporary source specifying its exact league designation is still being sought.

The 1947 Sachems went 7-3 and were led by Ernie Anganis, Sardi Nicolo, Eugene Decereau, and George Lasky. Lasky was the star of that 1947 team. Lasky won numerous awards through his High School career including the Sgt. Arthur Defranzo Player of the Year Award in 1946 and 1947, the Thomas Atkins Memorial Award in 1946, and was named to the Boston Globe, Boston Post, Lynn Item, and North Shore All Scholastic teams in 1947. The 1948 Sachems team had an off year going a disappointing 3-8.

The 1949 Sachems finished 10–1, sharing the North Shore championship with Gloucester and winning the Exchange Bowl against Weymouth, 7–6. Richie Nicolo’s 50-yard touchdown pass to his brother Sal “Sardi” Nicolo tied the bowl game, and Jimmy Kane’s extra point secured the victory. Co-captains Sardi Nicolo and Dan Murphy led a team also featuring Fred Quinlan and Richie Nicolo. Southward’s newspaper season wrap-up credits Sardi with an area-leading 99 points and 16 touchdowns and identifies Gloucester as Class B state champion. Conflicting team scoring totals in the supplied material require reconciliation, so no aggregate point total is asserted here. Sardi later played at LSU and scored on a 94-yard run against Rice on October 4, 1952.

Championship spotlight — 1949: John Janusas's 1949 Sachems went 10–1, shared the North Shore championship with Gloucester and won the Exchange Bowl in unforgettable fashion. Against Weymouth, Richie Nicolo connected with his brother Sal “Sardi” Nicolo on a 50-yard touchdown pass, and Jimmy Kane's extra point secured a 7–6 victory. Captains Sardi Nicolo and Dan Murphy helped lead a squad that brought enormous pride to Saugus. The superintendent's 1949 report singled out the Weymouth victory as a lasting community memory. This was an Exchange Bowl championship and North Shore co-title, not a documented Saugus state championship.

Saugus followed up their 1949 Championship season by going 8-2 and winning their second consecutive Exchange Bowl, this time a 30-12 victory over Brockton. Richie Nicolo was the star QB again and was helped by Charlie Murphy, Jim Driscoll, Leo Kane, Tony Serino, Charlie Woodell, and Ted Fredericks. This was Saugus’ second consecutive Exchange Bowl championship, marking the end of the Saugus Sachems Football Golden Era.

Championship spotlight — 1950: The 1950 Sachems followed their previous year's success with another Exchange Bowl championship, defeating Brockton 30–12 and finishing 8–2. Under John Janusas, Richie Nicolo again directed an accomplished team alongside Charlie Murphy, Jim Driscoll, Leo Kane, Tony Serino, Charlie Woodell and Ted Fredericks. The 1951 yearbook preserves the bowl victory and the team's achievements. Together, the 1949 and 1950 Exchange Bowl triumphs remain one of the proudest back-to-back accomplishments in Saugus football history.

The 1953 North Shore League champions finished 6–1–1 in regular-season play; the yearbook lists the Joyce Jamboree loss separately. Co-captains John Leahy and Doug MacNeill led the team, which clinched the title by beating Peabody 33–6 on Thanksgiving. The 1954 team followed with a 6–3 season under co-captains Jack Lawrence and Malcolm “Mal” Rice. The 1959 season records list a 6–2–1 finish and leading players David Matthews, Richie Burt and Jim Kelleher. The 1959 team is listed as North Shore League Champions, with the source qualification described in Championship Seasons.

Championship spotlight — 1953: John Janusas guided the 1953 Sachems to a 6–1–1 regular-season record and the North Shore League championship. Co-captains John Leahy and Doug MacNeill led the way, and a commanding 33–6 Thanksgiving victory over Peabody clinched the league crown. The 1954 yearbook explicitly connects that holiday victory to the championship and records the separate Joyce Jamboree loss outside the regular-season total. It was a fitting culmination to another strong season under Janusas.

Championship spotlight — 1959: The 1959 Sachems, coached by John Janusas, finished 6–2–1 and are remembered in the archive as North Shore League champions. David Matthews, Richie Burt and Jim Kelleher are among the team's noted players. Saugus Public Schools included the 1959 football squad among the championship teams recognized in its 2023 banner initiative, demonstrating the season's lasting place in school history. That announcement confirms championship recognition without specifying the exact historical league-title wording.
1961–1972 (Sustaining Competitiveness):
Bernard Stead (1961-1963)

Bernard Stead coached from 1961 through 1963. The season archive records finishes of 0–8, 1–8 and 0–9, respectively, a combined 1–25. Tom Carr is among the notable players listed for that period; the collection does not establish that he was its only All-Star.
Walter Sheridan (1964-1966)

Walter Sheridan coached from 1964 through 1966, culminating in a 7–2 season. The gallery’s 1967 yearbook pages identify the fall 1966 co-captains as Edward Maguire, John Dancewicz and Paul Uga, alongside Christie Serino, James Mancuso, Donald Murray, Richard Lombardo and their teammates. Four pages preserve the squad portrait, named player studies, game photographs, pep squad and cheerleaders. A conference championship has not been established by the reviewed sources. Serino later pursued a distinguished hockey coaching career, described in his alumni profile.
Paul Maguire (1967-1972)

Paul Maguire coached from 1967 through 1972. His 1969 Sachems finished 7–2 under captains John Richard, Richard Conti and William Babcock. The yearbook names Bob Osgood and Bill Eichel to the first offensive Northeastern Conference All-Star team and Steve Nelson to the first defensive team, with honorable mentions for Rich Desisto, Babcock, Conti and Richard. The only losses came against Class B champion Swampscott and Class A champion Peabody. Neither the successful record nor these individual honors establishes a Saugus conference championship; that claim remains unverified.
1973–1983: (The Ginolfi Era):
Mike Ginolfi (First tenure 1973-1983)
Mike “Gino” Ginolfi took over as the Sachems head coach in 1973. Coach Ginolfi restored Saugus as a competitive force.

The 1975 Sachems finished 9–1 and shared the Northeastern Conference championship. Captains Tom Heaney, Doug Mackie, John Nicolo and Steve Gannon led the team. The gallery preserves the 15–14 comeback against Salem and the muddy 6–0 Thanksgiving victory over Peabody. The 1978 yearbook’s review explicitly distinguishes the shared first-place finish in 1975 from the conference title won in 1977.

Championship spotlight — 1975: Mike “Gino” Ginolfi's 1975 Sachems delivered a 9–1 season and a share of first place in the Northeastern Conference. Captains Tom Heaney, Doug Mackie, John Nicolo and Steve Gannon helped drive the resurgence. Among the season's memorable moments were a 15–14 comeback against Salem and a hard-fought 6–0 Thanksgiving win over Peabody. Later yearbook coverage and local historical reporting both recall the shared conference finish, while the school district included the team in its championship-banner recognition.
Gannon went on to play college football at Holy Cross, being one of the program’s greatest players of all time. He is a member of both the Saugus High and Holy Cross Athletic Halls of Fame.

Doug Mackie earned high-school All-American recognition in 1975 and continued his football career at Ohio State. He later played in the USFL for the Tampa Bay Bandits and New Jersey Generals and appeared in the NFL for Atlanta. His alumni profile records additional time with the Giants and Saints. The gallery and alumni collection preserve his professional career; claims that he was the nation’s top recruit or that combine his 1984 All-Pro honor with Herschel Walker’s later rushing-record season require separate documentation.

Nicolo would go on to play college football at Ithaca College where in 1979 during his senior season, he would go on to be named a Division III All American and helped lead the Ithaca Bombers to a National Championship. Nicolo, who was also an excellent baseball player, led Ithaca’s Baseball team to the 1980 National Championship where he was named MVP. Nicolo would go on to play one year of minor league baseball in 1980 in the New York-Penn League for the Auburn Americans (who were affiliated with the Los Angeles Dodgers and Cleveland Indians). Nicolo would go on to be inducted into the Ithaca College Athletic Hall of Fame as a player in 1986 and twice more with both National Championship Teams. This led to Saugus creating their own Athletic Hall of Fame in 1987, by his father-in-law, Dr. John Mangini, which included the following Sachems Football players in their Inaugural Class: John Nicolo, Sardi Nicolo, Christie Serino, Doug Mackie, George Laskey, Stan Green, John “Iron Mike” Harrington, and Art Spinney.

The Sachems followed a 2–8 season in 1976 with a 9–1 Northeastern Conference championship in 1977. The yearbook identifies co-captains Dan Hashem and Frank Doyle and senior contributors including George Nicolo, Frank Serino, Paul Serino, John Coffey and Tim Fawcett. A 12–10 Thanksgiving win over Peabody closed the season. The gallery also preserves Mike Ginolfi’s 1977 Item Coach of the Year recognition.

Championship spotlight — 1977: Two years after sharing the conference crown, Mike Ginolfi's 1977 Sachems won the Northeastern Conference outright with a 9–1 record. Captains Dan Hashem and Frank Doyle led a talented squad that included George Nicolo, Frank Serino, Paul Serino, John Coffey and Tim Fawcett. A 12–10 Thanksgiving victory over Peabody provided a memorable finish, and the gallery preserves Ginolfi's 1977 Lynn Item Coach of the Year recognition. Contemporary yearbook material and later local reporting distinguish this outright title from the 1975 co-championship.

Saugus finished 6–3–1 in 1978 and 5–5 in both 1979 and 1980. The 1978 yearbook identifies returning starters Paul Nigro, Don Trainor, Bill Peach and Mike Allen. Steve Peach became a three-time Lynn Item All-Star and later played at Syracuse and Boston College, where he also punted. The gallery’s 1980 review recalls a 40–6 Thanksgiving victory over Peabody. These season summaries should be distinguished from individual alumni achievements.

The 1981 Sachems season was the worst season for Ginolfi during his first tenure as they went 1-9. Saugus bounced back in 1982 going 5-4-1. That season Saugus was led by Steve Fauci, Anthony Cogliano, Mark Strange, and Anthony Guthro. 1983 Saugus fell back to below .500 going 4-6. The team was led by Tom Trainor, Kevin Pelley, and Bob Cinelli.

Ginolfi would step down after the 1983 season and moved into athletic administration. His coaching tree shaped Saugus football for decades through assistants and former players who followed him into the head coaching role.
1984–1993: Inconsistency and Brief Success
Kevin Ward (1984-1990)

Kevin Ward took over in 1984, and the program went through several down years, though the 1987 team rebounded to go 7-3. A reported shared Northeastern Conference title remains unverified; no supporting contemporary clipping has been located. Marc Fauci emerged as one of the Sachems greatest players. He was named Boston Globe All Scholastic in 1989. Fauci would go on to play college football at Boston University (BU). While at BU, Fauci would play Linebacker and was twice named Co-Captain as a junior and senior. Fauci led BU to arguably its best season ever in 1993 when they went 12-1 and finished the regular season with a perfect 11-0 mark, the first unbeaten and untied record in program history. Fauci was named a second-team All-America by The Sports Network and National Weekly Football Gazette and a third-team All-America selection by the Associated Press.
Mike “Bonty” Bontempo (1991-1993)

The 1990 team went 8-2, which was Saugus’s best record in years. After that, Mike “Bonty” Bontempo took over and coached through 1993, but the program struggled during that span going 1-29. During his tenure he coached All Stars Sean Publicover and Joe Attubato.
1994–2004: Rebuilding and Setbacks
Mike Ginolfi (Second Tenure 1994-1995)

Mike Ginolfi returned in 1994. After an 0–10 season, the 1995 Sachems snapped a 34-game losing streak with a 25–0 victory over Winthrop and finished 6–5, their first winning season since 1990. Co-captain Mike Mabee, a multi-sport standout, led the team with L.J. McKanas, Carlo Abate, Matt Nazzaro and Derek Bilton. The gallery preserves the streak-ending game and the 50–20 win over Lynn English that clinched a winning season. An early-season Boston Herald clipping ranked Saugus No. 16; that was not a final-season ranking.

Coach Ginolfi retired from coaching after the 1995 season. He will always be remembered as one of the greatest football coaches in Sachem history, as he was a 1993 Saugus High Athletic Hall of Fame inductee, but he was also one of the greatest coaches in Massachusetts Football History as he was inducted into the Massachusetts High School Football Coaches Association Hall of Fame in 1992. Coach Ginolfi would remain Athletic Director at Saugus until he retired from that position in 2002
John Fauci (1996-1998)

John Fauci took over for Coach Ginolfi for the 1996 season. Saugus finished the 1996 season with a 4–7 record. The Sachems were led by John Plunkett, Justin Falite, and LJ McKanas. McKanas would be named to numerous All-Star teams as a RB. He would go on to play college football at Northeastern. While at Northeastern McKanas would go on to set numerous rushing records. During his Senior season in 2001 McKanas set records for most carries, 342, rushing yards, 1756, and rushing touchdowns, 14. He gained over 100 yards rushing in nine games and over 200 in three. He averaged 5.1 yards per carry and 159.6 per game as the team posted a 5-6 record. His 242 rushing yards against Massachusetts is second in the Husky record books. He won numerous awards, including All-New England, All-Conference and first-team Hanson All-America. He also received the Harry Agganis Award as the Outstanding Senior Football Player in New England. In 2009 he was inducted into the Northeastern Athletic Hall of Fame. McKanas later was a contestant on the popular TV Show Survivor. His alumni profile records a ninth-place finish. He was the first of two former Sachems to become a contestant on the popular reality show.

Saugus finished 6–4–1 in 1997 and 5–6 in 1998. The 1998 Thanksgiving preview credits Raphael Zammit with 21 total touchdowns before the finale—18 rushing, two receiving and one interception return—surpassing the previous total-touchdown mark of 20 credited to L.J. McKanas. That total-touchdown distinction should not be confused with a rushing-touchdown record. The same preview highlights quarterback Ryan Lahey (Leahy in the season workbook), Mike Panzini and their teammates; its figures are pre-Thanksgiving totals rather than confirmed final-season statistics.
Dean Sacca (1999-2000)

Dean Sacca became head coach in 1999. The 1999 season had a promising start as Saugus started the year 3-3 however Saugus would end the year 3-8. All Star George Lowe, who played almost every skilled position that year, led the team along with Brian Mirasolo. The Sachems continued to struggle in the 2000 season by going 2-8. Coach Sacca stepped down at the end of the season. Ryan Gould was the only All-Star from the 2000 team.
John Nicolo (2001-2004)

John Nicolo took over as the Sachems Head Coach in 2001. Unfortunately, Coach Nicolo’s tenure did not produce the same success as he had during his playing days. The 2001 Sachems went 2-9 and were led by Pat Quinlan, Patrick Eaton, and Kyle Sucharewicz. The 2002 Sachems went 1-10 and were led by Sal Nicolo and All-Star Anthony Barbanti. Sal Nicolo would go on to play two seasons of college football for Division III Bridgewater State Bears under Peter Mazzaferro.

The 2003 Sachems finished 3–8. Junior running back Mike Nicolo rushed for 1,462 yards and 11 touchdowns and set the then Saugus single-game rushing record with 306 yards against Salem, as documented in the gallery and alumni profile. Anthony “Beave” Barbanti’s senior profile records 75 tackles, 11 tackles for loss and three sacks, alongside his work on the offensive line. Mark Spadafora and Chris Benson also feature in the season entry.

The 2004 Sachems were plagued with injuries to their core players and the promising rebuild came to a stop as they finished the season 0-11. Nicolo missed part of the season and played most of the season with an injured knee and shoulder. Despite the injuries Nicolo was still named an All-Star along with teammate Brian Bianchi. Mike Nicolo would go on to play College Football for New England Division III power Curry College however injuries followed him throughout his college career. Nicolo was inducted into the Curry College Athletic Hall of Fame as a member of the 2007 Curry Football Team, which was ranked 19th Nationally and had won 4-consecutive New England Football Conference Championships.
After the 2004 season, Coach Nicolo stepped down as Head Coach and took on the role of Athletic Director.
2005–2016: (The Broderick Era)
Mike Broderick (2005-2016)

Mike Broderick took over in 2005 and brought stability back to the program. Coach Broderick was the first Sachems Head Coach to have not been under the Ginolfi Coaching Tree since the Paul Maguire days.

Coach Broderick’s first two seasons were rebuilding seasons for the Sachems. His 2005 team went 1-10, led by All Star Alex Klimarchuk. In 2006 the Sachems improved to 3-7. Although the record didn’t seem like much, this team was remembered for becoming the first Saugus team to defeat the Sachems Thanksgiving Day rival, the Peabody Tanners, for the first time in 18 seasons. That Sachems team was led by senior All Star, Rodney Lavoie, who went on to be a contestant on the TV Show Survivor in 2015, the second former Sachem to appear on the hit TV Show. Saugus also had a freshman QB by the name of Mike DiChiaria who had a breakout season. DiChiaria would transfer to the prep school BB&N to finish out his High School career, where DiChiaria made the top 10 in Massachusetts state history for career touchdown passes. He would go on to play college football at Cornell.

In 2007 Saugus took a major step forward and had their first winning season since 1997, going 7-3. The 2007 team was led by Paul Sullivan and All Stars Tyler Trainor, Mike Dean, and Brett Reid. The 2008 team also went 7-3 and were again led by All Stars Mike Dean and Brett Reid.

From 2009 through 2011, the Sachems fell back to below .500. Although these teams didn’t have as much success, they still had some All-Star players like Shamir Guillaume and AJ Guthro. Guillaume would go on to set the Sachems single season rushing yards record by rushing for 1,678 yards in 2010.

The Sachems finished 6–5 in 2012 and 3–8 in 2013, following the season table. Tom Trainor, C.J. Randolph, Nick Benoit and Ismael Minaya are listed for 2012. Justin Winn earned junior-season All-Scholastic recognition in 2013. His 2013 rushing total differs between the supplied statistics table and alumni text; those figures require source-level reconciliation.

In 2014, Saugus finished 6–5. Dan Cacciola’s 375-yard, four-touchdown game against Winthrop surpassed Mike Nicolo’s earlier 306-yard single-game mark. The statistics table records 1,467 rushing yards and 18 rushing touchdowns for Cacciola, and 1,255 yards and 22 rushing touchdowns for Justin Winn. The archive describes Winn’s 22 rushing touchdowns as a school record. Cacciola’s surname appears as Cicciola in parts of the supplied workbook; the gallery and statistics section use Cacciola.

Saugus finished 3–9–1 in 2015 and 1–10 in 2016, as listed in the season archive. Brendan Grocki and Cam Williamson appear among the notable players for those teams. Mike Broderick’s tenure ended after the 2016 season, concluding twelve seasons as head coach.
2017 onward: Nalen, Mabee, Cummings and Bluestein
Anthony Nalen (2017)

Anthony Nalen was hired in 2017, and Saugus improved from the previous season. Ricky Martinez helped lead the Sachems. Unfortunately, due to a controversy during the 2018 off-season, Nalen was removed as head coach.
Mike Mabee (2018)

After Nalen’s departure, former Sachems great and former player under Coach Ginolfi, Mike Mabee, was hired to serve as interim Head Coach. Coach Mabee was able to guide a competitive team to a 4-7 record. The team was led by All-Star Dante McGrane.
Steve Cummings (2019–2025)

The Sachems under Coach Cummings have seen their ups and downs. The Sachems took a step back during the 2019 season when they went 3-8. The team was led by All Star Marvens Jean as well as Kyle Surette, Sal Franco, Christian Correa, and Javier Martinez.
The 2020 Season was interrupted by the Covid-19 Pandemic, but Saugus was still able to play a 7 game schedule during the season, going 2-5.

The season archive records 0–11 in 2021 and 2–11 in 2022. These supplied totals require schedule-level confirmation. Mike MacEacheran and Braden Faiella are among the players recorded during this period.

The 2023 Sachems finished 5–6. Braden Faiella, Tommy DeSimmone and Dylan Clark are listed among the season’s leading players. The gallery’s senior Faiella profile reports 140 tackles and a career total of 482, and credits him with Item Defensive Player of the Year recognition. The coach’s suggestion that the career total might be a state record is not treated as a verified record. Faiella later continued his football career at Saint Anselm; the supplied workbook also spells his first name Brandon.
The 2024 Sachems went 3-8 and were led by All Stars Koby Jette and Cody Munafo.

The supplied sources disagree on the 2025 record: the written history lists 2–9, while the later honors, alumni and statistics workbook lists 3–8. Koby Jette appears in the supplied player honors. A final schedule is needed before resolving the team record.
Greg Bluestein (2026–present)
Saugus High named alumnus and former assistant Greg Bluestein head football coach in February 2026, succeeding Steve Cummings after seven seasons.
Conclusion

Saugus football has a proud and deeply rooted history. While the program has not reached the heights of its golden era in recent times, it has produced championship caliber teams, conference titles, and many memorable players who excelled at the college and professional levels. More than wins and losses, being a Sachem has always meant pride, tradition, and commitment to the red and white.
